attacks.claim: Self-update trusts a key compiled into the binary, but the plan never says how the key is rotated, revoked, or how a compromised signing key is handled. It also does not say whether the signature covers the version/tag, so a validly signed older archive could be served as 'latest' (downgrade/rollback attack) to users running --version.
attacks.evidence: "The minisign public key is compiled into the binary; the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies." ABSENT: key rotation/revocation plan, anti-downgrade check, and whether the signature covers version metadata.

attacks.claim: The update path fetches release metadata from the GitHub API over HTTPS but the plan does not define checks on redirect targets, maximum download size, or how the archive is unpacked (path traversal in tar extraction into the install dir). Signature verification must happen before any extraction and the extraction logic is unspecified.
attacks.evidence: "Downloads the platform archive and its .minisig signature... Writes the new binary to a temp file in the same directory" ABSENT: archive-extraction safety rules, size limits, and ordering of verify-before-extract.

attacks.claim: The install ID is a persistent random identifier stored locally and sent with every daily POST, making installs linkable across days and across the command/backend/OS fingerprint. The plan's consent text and docs do not disclose that the ID is persistent or how users reset it, and the 'anonymous' label is overstated.
attacks.evidence: "a random install ID generated locally" and consent prompt "Share anonymous usage stats" ABSENT: install ID lifetime, reset/deletion command, retention on the collector side, and disclosure that the ID is persistent.

attacks.claim: The collector's ingest log (IP address, timestamp, user agent) is not addressed. Discarding raw events after aggregation does not cover the VPS web server access logs, which capture source IPs for every POST and would make the opt-in data re-identifiable.
attacks.evidence: "writing daily aggregate counts only (raw events discarded after aggregation)" ABSENT: handling of source IPs in access logs, retention period, and log rotation policy.

attacks.claim: Telemetry is enabled by a prompt on an interactive run, but the consent flow and default for existing users after an upgrade is unspecified for GDPR-style standards: a prompt that defaults to No is fine, but there is no record of consent or withdrawal beyond the config, and no legal review is mentioned. Also the plan has no data processing terms for the VPS.
attacks.evidence: "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once" ABSENT: legal review, consent record, and data-processing basis for the donated VPS.

attacks.claim: Atomic self-replace and kvx.prev rollback can leave the install broken if the process is interrupted between the two renames, and the plan does not define a recovery step. Also, on Windows an in-use binary cannot be replaced by rename, yet the plan targets Windows only as a service exclusion.
attacks.evidence: "atomic rename over the current binary. The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev" ABSENT: crash-between-renames recovery, and Windows self-replacement behaviour.

attacks.claim: Telemetry and update-check failures are dropped silently with no observability, so ops cannot tell whether the collector is receiving data or whether the 75% target is measurable at all.
attacks.evidence: "failures are dropped, never retried in the foreground" ABSENT: metrics or alerting for collector ingestion health.

attacks.claim: The motivating 41% figure is a download-count tally, but download counts from GitHub include mirrors, CI pulls, and Homebrew/apt caches, so they do not measure running-version share. The success target (59% to 75%) is therefore computed on a metric that cannot show users running old versions, and the baseline 59% is not shown as derived from the same method.
attacks.evidence: "41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2 (GitHub release download counts, tallied per asset)" and "share of downloads on the latest minor version >= 75% (from 59%)"

attacks.claim: The 78 combined thumbs-up is used as demand evidence but the issues are not shown to request telemetry, and the backend-prioritisation claim is unprototyped: no estimate of how many opt-in users will exist, so the data may be too sparse to prioritise anything.
attacks.evidence: "Issues #812, #845, #903 ask for 'kvx self-update' (78 combined thumbs-up)." ABSENT: sample-size estimate for opt-in telemetry.

attacks.claim: The collector runs on a donated VPS with no capacity, bandwidth, or abuse analysis. At ~14,000 weekly downloads, a one-POST-per-day-per-install design is bounded, but any forged or replayed traffic is unthrottled and no rate limit is defined.
attacks.evidence: "a ~150-line Go service on the project's existing donated VPS" ABSENT: rate limiting, auth on the ingest endpoint, or capacity estimate.

attacks.claim: The telemetry ingest endpoint is unauthenticated and the plan does not say how the collector rejects spoofed or junk payloads, so anyone can inflate the published 'stats/' aggregates that the maintainers use to prioritise backends.
attacks.evidence: "Collector: a ~150-line Go service ... Aggregates are published monthly in the repo under stats/." ABSENT: ingest authentication, payload validation, or anomaly filtering.

attacks.claim: The 24-hour startup-check throttle and the telemetry daily POST need a stored timestamp, but the plan does not say where state is stored or how concurrent kvx invocations avoid races on that file.
attacks.evidence: "at most once per 24 h" and "at most one POST per day" ABSENT: state file location and concurrency handling.

attacks.claim: The startup notice and the telemetry consent prompt both appear on interactive runs, so a new user may see two prompts in the same session on first upgrade, adding friction.
attacks.evidence: "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once" and startup notice "at most once per 24 h" ABSENT: ordering or suppression rule between the two prompts.

attacks.claim: The consent prompt is a single-line text question with a [y/N] convention; the plan does not address screen-reader phrasing or non-English locales.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)? [y/N]" ABSENT: localisation or accessibility notes.

attacks.claim: Self-update, package-manager detection, telemetry client and collector are scoped to 3 weeks for 2 maintainers, with the collector and docs compressed into week 3 alongside the rc1 soak. Scope is tight with no contingency.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: collector service, docs/telemetry.md, release notes, v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0." ABSENT: contingency or scope cut plan.

attacks.claim: Telemetry data already sent cannot be recalled, and the plan does not say what happens to aggregates already published if a user later withdraws consent or if a privacy defect is found in the payload schema.
attacks.evidence: "Changeable any time: kvx telemetry on|off|status" ABSENT: deletion or retraction path for already-sent data.

attacks.claim: Not analysed: at 10–100x download growth the daily POST load and aggregate storage grow linearly; the plan gives no load estimate.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: load estimate for the collector and the GitHub API call volume from the startup check at scale (each check is an unauthenticated GitHub API request subject to rate limits).

attacks.claim: The collector and update channel both depend on GitHub Releases and GitHub API availability, and the telemetry lives on a single donated VPS with no documented exit path.
attacks.evidence: "distributed via GitHub Releases" and "donated VPS" ABSENT: fallback or migration path if either provider or the VPS goes away.

attacks.claim: Nothing unusual to the rendering of output; the single stderr notice line is plain text.
attacks.evidence: nothing

attacks.claim: The plan says telemetry is for prioritising backends, but the payload includes exit-code class and kvx version, which the plan does not justify as needed for that decision.
attacks.evidence: "exit code class (ok/user-error/internal-error), kvx version" ABSENT: justification tying each field to the prioritisation decision.

attacks.claim: The payload field 'command name' combined with 'backend type' and OS/arch may still be a quasi-identifier for small deployments; the 'complete list' claim should be checked against k-anonymity expectations for the published aggregates.
attacks.evidence: "Payload (complete list, documented in docs/telemetry.md)"

attacks.claim: Self-update trust rests only on a single minisign key compiled into the binary with no documented rotation or revocation path, and the plan does not say whether the signature covers the version/tag so that a validly signed older archive could be replayed as an 'update' (downgrade attack back to a vulnerable version such as v2.6.2).
attacks.evidence: "the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies. The same key already signs our releases today" — no mention of version binding, anti-rollback, or key rotation.

attacks.claim: The self-update path fetches metadata from the GitHub Releases API and selects 'latest non-prerelease' with no pinned channel or check that the release is signed by the expected key before choosing a version; a compromised or spoofed API response determines which artifact is downloaded. Also --version vX.Y.Z accepts arbitrary tags including old vulnerable ones.
attacks.evidence: "--version vX.Y.Z" and "Queries the GitHub Releases API for the latest non-prerelease tag"

attacks.claim: Rollback keeps kvx.prev, a previously-valid binary that may be vulnerable; there is no statement that kvx.prev is itself verified before swap, and it sits in the same writable directory.
attacks.evidence: "The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev; kvx self-update --rollback swaps them back."

attacks.claim: The telemetry payload includes a persistent random install ID; combined with OS/arch, kvx version and timestamps at daily granularity, this makes users linkable over time. The plan does not say the ID is rotatable/deletable on 'off', nor what the collector logs (IP addresses at the VPS web server are unaddressed and would be retained by default).
attacks.evidence: "a random install ID generated locally" and "Collector: a ~150-line Go service on the project's existing donated VPS" — no ID reset, no IP-handling or access-log policy.

attacks.claim: Consent is captured once but the plan does not say whether consent is recorded or re-prompted after the payload schema changes, which would be a material change to what is collected.
attacks.evidence: "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once"

attacks.claim: Startup update check sends an HTTPS GET to GitHub on every eligible run, disclosing IP and kvx version; this is not in the telemetry consent and is not described as a data flow.
attacks.evidence: "The check is a single HTTPS GET with a 1.5 s timeout"

attacks.claim: Telemetry collector and update distribution depend on GitHub and a single donated VPS; there is no stated self-hosting option for the collector or an exit plan if the donor withdraws.
attacks.evidence: "on the project's existing donated VPS"

attacks.claim: Collector sizing is unstated: a single 150-line service on one VPS with no load estimate for ~14,000 weekly downloads growing with adoption, and no rate limiting on the POST endpoint, which is open to anyone who finds it.
attacks.evidence: "a ~150-line Go service on the project's existing donated VPS"

attacks.claim: No budget or bandwidth estimate for the GitHub API calls and 12 MB archive downloads triggered by self-update and rc testing; unauthenticated GitHub API rate limits (60/h per IP) could cause failures for users behind shared NAT, and this is unaddressed.
attacks.evidence: "Queries the GitHub Releases API" — no token, rate-limit handling, or caching described.

attacks.claim: The telemetry collector and the aggregate publishing have no defined failure or ops owner; a 3-week build with two maintainers ships a new public-facing service with no monitoring, alerting, or on-call expectation, and the success metric depends on it working.
attacks.evidence: "Collector: a ~150-line Go service" and "Aggregates are published monthly in the repo under stats/" — no monitoring or ownership stated.

attacks.claim: Self-update atomic replace is described for the same directory but the plan does not address Windows (rename over a running executable fails) even though Windows is mentioned in out-of-scope, leaving an unhandled platform.
attacks.evidence: "atomic rename over the current binary"

attacks.claim: Telemetry transmission and the consent prompt are one-way: data already sent cannot be recalled, and the plan does not define deletion of already-collected aggregates or raw events in transit, nor a path to withdraw the install ID server-side.
attacks.evidence: "Changeable any time: kvx telemetry on|off|status" — 'off' is described only for future sending.

attacks.claim: The 'Package-manager installs' refusal rule is underspecified and can misfire: symlinks (e.g. /usr/local/bin/kvx pointing into a Cellar) and binaries installed manually to /usr/bin with no dpkg ownership are not addressed; the check on dpkg/rpm ownership also needs to handle rpm which has no simple file-ownership query without the rpm database.
attacks.evidence: "if the binary path is under a Homebrew Cellar or is owned by the dpkg/rpm database"

attacks.claim: Consent prompt default and the TTY/CI rule conflict with the 'never delays' claim: the consent prompt blocks the command on first interactive run, which contradicts the statement that startup behaviour never delays the command.
attacks.evidence: "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once" vs "it never delays the command"

attacks.claim: The motivating 41% figure and the success target baseline (59%) are asserted without a method shown; the 41% is derived from per-asset download counts, which include mirrors, CI pulls and package-manager fetches, and the plan does not reconcile that these are not user-version counts. Also the claim that equal effort across backends leaves usage unknown is not evidenced.
attacks.evidence: "41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2 (GitHub release download counts, tallied per asset)" and "share of downloads on the latest minor version >= 75% (from 59%)"

attacks.claim: Opt-in telemetry will be a biased sample; the backend-prioritisation decision rests on it, yet no caveat or plan to weight or validate against the download data is stated.
attacks.evidence: "Backend prioritisation is currently guesswork" — no sampling-bias treatment in Section 3 or 7.

attacks.claim: Telemetry collecting OS/arch and version with a persistent ID may fall under GDPR/PECR consent and data-subject rights for EU users; the plan does not address a lawful basis, the right to erasure, or a privacy notice beyond docs/telemetry.md.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats" — 'anonymous' is asserted with a persistent random install ID, not analysed.

attacks.claim: Telemetry prompt in the first interactive run adds friction on every upgrade path and the 'y/N' default is acceptable, but the self-update notice at most once per 24h is unmeasured against the stated goal.
attacks.evidence: "asks once" — no check of prompt fatigue or dismissal behaviour.

attacks.claim: Consent prompt and update notice are single-line stderr/stdin text with no described non-colour or screen-reader consideration; the plan does not address the prompt's readability with assistive tech beyond TTY detection.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)? [y/N]"

attacks.claim: The one-line update notice and consent prompt have no specified copy beyond the quoted strings; no review of wording or localisation.
attacks.evidence: ""kvx vX.Y.Z available (kvx self-update)"

attacks.claim: The plan assumes users want auto-notified self-update; the issues cited ask for the command, not for notifications or telemetry, so the telemetry and notice scope may solve a problem users did not request.
attacks.evidence: "Issues #812, #845, #903 ask for "kvx self-update""

attacks.claim: Self-update, package-manager detection, telemetry client, consent flow and a separate collector service are bundled into one 3-week, two-person plan with a release gate, increasing coupling and scope risk.
attacks.evidence: "Maintainers: 2 | 3 weeks | Target release: v2.8.0"

attacks.claim: The plan commits to a v2.8.0 release with a 1-week RC and a new public service and signing-path changes, but does not state rollback criteria if the RC reveals a self-update bug on a platform, which matters because a broken self-update can strand users on a version they cannot replace.
attacks.evidence: "v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0" — no rollback or abort criteria.

attacks.claim: Self-update fetches the archive and signature from GitHub Releases and verifies with a compiled-in key, but the plan never says the signature covers the exact binary being installed, nor that the signing key has rotation/revocation or compromise handling. If the minisign key is compromised, every installed kvx will accept malicious updates with no recovery path short of manual reinstall.
attacks.evidence: "The minisign public key is compiled into the binary; the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies. The same key already signs our releases today"

attacks.claim: The --version flag and rollback path are not specified to enforce downgrade protection, so an attacker who can get a validly signed older release (e.g. v2.6.2 with the credential-logging bug) can make users install vulnerable versions via --version. Signature validity alone does not prevent rollback attacks.
attacks.evidence: "kvx self-update [--check] [--version vX.Y.Z]"

attacks.claim: Release-metadata trust is not stated: the version is chosen from the GitHub Releases API response and the .minisig is fetched from the same channel, with no pinning of the signature to a specific tag or TLS/host verification described.
attacks.evidence: "Queries the GitHub Releases API for the latest non-prerelease tag"

attacks.claim: The install ID is a persistent random identifier that links all of a user's runs across time and, combined with version and OS/arch, is a stable linkable identifier. The plan does not state rotation, deletion on opt-out, or whether the ID is reset when telemetry is turned off, so 'anonymous' is overstated. Also the startup update check reveals IP and version to GitHub/collector on every run, with no consent.
attacks.evidence: "a random install ID generated locally (not derived from hostname, user, or MAC)"

attacks.claim: The collector receives client IP addresses at the VPS web layer; the plan says raw events are discarded but does not say request logs (which contain IPs) are excluded or rotated.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention and log handling for the collector's HTTP access logs on the donated VPS

attacks.claim: The consent prompt is not a legally adequate notice under GDPR/ePrivacy-style rules for a persistent identifier: it does not state the controller, legal basis, retention period, or the right to withdraw beyond a one-line toggle. Opt-in itself is good, but the notice is thin for a published open-source project with EU users.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)? [y/N]"

attacks.claim: The update check and self-update both contact GitHub on every run without disclosure in the consent story; the Homebrew/dpkg refusal logic and binary replacement may conflict with platform/distribution policies if the binary is installed system-wide.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: disclosure of the update-check network call in the startup notice or docs

attacks.claim: Self-update atomically replaces the running binary and keeps only one kvx.prev. A bad release that passes signature check but breaks startup leaves the user with a broken binary and no automatic recovery; rollback is a manual command that itself runs the broken binary's code path (the new binary handles --rollback). Also, rollback after two successive updates loses the known-good version.
attacks.evidence: "The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev; kvx self-update --rollback swaps them back."

attacks.claim: No plan for a failed or partial update beyond temp-file-then-rename: a crash between writing kvx.prev and the rename, or a permission failure after the rename on some filesystems, can leave the install in an inconsistent state. The plan also lacks a health check on the new binary before committing.
attacks.evidence: "Writes the new binary to a temp file in the same directory, fsyncs, then atomic rename over the current binary."

attacks.claim: The 2 s telemetry POST and 1.5 s update check are fire-and-forget with no mention of observability: there is no way for maintainers to know the collector is down or that the rate of dropped events is high, and the plan has no alerting for the VPS collector.
attacks.evidence: "failures are dropped, never retried in the foreground"

attacks.claim: Telemetry at one POST per install per day against a single ~150-line service on a donated VPS has no capacity analysis; 14,000 weekly downloads implies the collector must absorb all opted-in installs' daily traffic, and no rate limiting or auth exists to prevent abuse of a public endpoint.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: request volume estimate, rate limiting, or abuse protection for the collector endpoint

attacks.claim: Update delivery depends on GitHub Releases; the telemetry collector depends on one donated VPS with no documented exit or handover plan if the donor withdraws.
attacks.evidence: "on the project's existing donated VPS"

attacks.claim: No budget math for bandwidth on the donated VPS for full-archive downloads (< 12 MB each) by users checking for updates, though the plan does not route update downloads through the VPS, so cost risk is low; the collector's egress and any storage of aggregates is unquantified.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: bandwidth and storage estimate for the collector

attacks.claim: The motivating 41% figure and the 59% baseline are asserted without a cited query or dataset, and the success target (75% on latest minor) is set without any prototype; GitHub download counts are not a reliable proxy for installed version, so the success measure may not be measurable as stated.
attacks.evidence: "41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2"

attacks.claim: The claim that backend prioritisation is guesswork is an unproven premise; telemetry opt-in rates (likely low given default-off) may yield a sample too biased to prioritise backends, and the plan does not say how biased samples will be handled.
attacks.evidence: "Backend prioritisation is currently guesswork"

attacks.claim: The startup notice and first-run consent prompt add interactive friction to the first run after upgrade; the plan does not describe how the consent prompt interacts with scripts that run kvx with a TTY but in non-interactive loops.
attacks.evidence: "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once"

attacks.claim: The 'at most once per 24 h' update notice has no specified storage location or behavior when the state file is unwritable, and the telemetry 'at most one POST per day' has no specified clock or timezone boundary, which could produce duplicate or missed daily sends.
attacks.evidence: "at most once per 24 h"

attacks.claim: The package-manager detection relies on path heuristics (Homebrew Cellar, dpkg/rpm ownership) that differ across distros and Linux installs under /usr/local; the test matrix does not cover those paths.
attacks.evidence: "if the binary path is under a Homebrew Cellar or is owned by the dpkg/rpm database"

attacks.claim: The update-available notice and the telemetry prompt both write to stderr/stdout in an unspecified format; the copy for the consent prompt is given but the update notice copy has no review for misleading wording about what 'available' means for package-managed installs.
attacks.evidence: "kvx vX.Y.Z available (kvx self-update)"

attacks.claim: The consent prompt uses a bracketed [y/N] default with no mention of screen-reader-friendly output or an accessible alternative; the plan does not address it.

The plan dispatches a 3-week build to 2 maintainers with a week-3 release-candidate cycle, yet the collector, docs, release notes and rc soak all fall into week 3 with no slack; a single slip ships v2.8.0 without the telemetry or the rollback tests.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: collector service, docs/telemetry.md, release notes, v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0."
